events.title: Roman conquest of Dacia
hints: An emperor's victory over a king in AD 106 is told in a spiral relief on a column in Rome.
The province's mines paid for the emperor's building works.
events.summary: Emperor Trajan conquered the Dacian kingdom in two wars, in AD 101–102 and 105–106, and made it a province. Its gold and silver mines and salt were exploited until the Romans withdrew around 271.

events.title: Ottoman suzerainty over Wallachia
hints: A principality kept its own prince but paid annual tribute to a distant sultan.
Its grain and livestock helped feed a faraway imperial capital.
events.summary: Wallachia became a tributary of the Ottoman Empire from 1417 and, with neighbouring Moldavia, remained under Ottoman suzerainty for centuries. Tribute and compulsory grain and livestock deliveries fed Istanbul until independence was recognised in 1878.
events.quip: The sultan collected the tribute; the princes kept the title and the paperwork.

events.title: Habsburg annexation of Bukovina
hints: A neighbouring empire occupied the northern part of a principality in 1775 and later claimed it by treaty.
Its capital was Czernowitz, a multicultural university city.
events.summary: In 1775 the Habsburg Monarchy occupied the northern part of the Principality of Moldavia, called Bukovina, and the Ottomans formally ceded it. It remained a Habsburg crown land with its capital at Czernowitz until 1918.

events.title: Russian annexation of Bessarabia
hints: A treaty signed at Bucharest in 1812 gave the tsar the eastern half of a principality.
The territory between the Prut and the Dniester was renamed after a southern dynasty.
events.summary: The Treaty of Bucharest in 1812 transferred the eastern half of the Principality of Moldavia to the Russian Empire, which called it Bessarabia. It was part of the empire until 1918, and its status was disputed in the 20th century.

events.title: German occupation and oil concessions in the First World War
hints: Wartime occupation seized oilfields to fuel a rival empire's war machine.
A harsh 1918 peace treaty handed the occupier control over oil and grain.
events.summary: After entering the First World War in 1916, the country was overrun by the Central Powers. Germany took over the Ploiești oilfields and wheat harvests, and the 1918 Treaty of Bucharest imposed heavy economic terms before it was voided after the armistice.

events.title: German economic control in the Second World War
hints: A trade treaty in 1939 swapped arms for oil on terms dictated by a larger partner.
Refineries at Ploiesti were a main target of Allied bombers in 1943.
events.summary: A 1939 economic treaty and later agreements tied Romania's oil and grain exports to German armaments, and Ploiesti oil became vital to the German war effort. Romania joined the Axis in 1940 and switched sides in August 1944.
events.quip: A commercial treaty in which one party chose the goods, the prices and the delivery schedule.

events.title: Soviet annexation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina
hints: A June 1940 ultimatum demanded territory within days.
A secret protocol signed with another dictator had pre-agreed the carve-up.
events.summary: In June 1940 the Soviet Union issued an ultimatum demanding Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina. Under the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the territory was ceded within days and later absorbed into the Soviet republics.
events.wikipediaTitle: Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina

events.title: Second Vienna Award
hints: Arbitrators from Berlin and Rome divided a region in August 1940 after pressure from Moscow's gains.
Roughly two fifths of a historic region went to a revisionist neighbour.
events.summary: Under the Second Vienna Award of 30 August 1940, decided by Germany and Italy, Romania ceded Northern Transylvania to Hungary. Romania regained the territory in 1944–45.

events.title: Soviet occupation and economic extraction
hints: Armistice terms demanded huge reparations paid in kind.
Joint "Sov" companies siphoned off its oil.
events.summary: After the August 1944 coup the Red Army occupied the country, and the armistice required heavy reparations in goods. Joint Soviet-run SovRom companies controlled oil and other sectors until the mid-1950s, and Soviet troops withdrew in 1958.
events.quip: Joint ventures: where one partner contributes the oil and the other contributes the enthusiasm.
